title: Linear Programming
summary: Linear programming finds the best (maximum or minimum) value of a linear objective function subject to linear constraints. This chapter covers formulating a problem, drawing the feasible region and solving by the corner point method.

notes.heading: Meaning and terminology
notes.html:
• Linear programming problem (LPP): optimise a linear function of variables subject to linear inequalities.
  • Decision variables: the unknown quantities x, y to be decided.
  • Objective function: Z = ax + by, to be maximised (profit) or minimised (cost).
  • Constraints: linear inequalities expressing limited resources or requirements.
  • Non-negativity restrictions: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
  • Feasible region: the common region satisfying all constraints. Any point in it is a feasible solution.
  • Optimal solution: a feasible solution giving the best value of Z.

notes.heading: Formulating an LPP
notes.html:
1. Identify the decision variables and name them x and y.
  2. Write the objective function Z in terms of x and y.
  3. Convert each condition into an inequality: 'at most / not more than' gives ≤, 'at least / not less than' gives ≥.
  4. Add x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

Example 1

A firm makes products A and B. A needs 2 machine-hours and 1 labour-hour; B needs 1 machine-hour and 3 labour-hours. Available: 40 machine-hours and 45 labour-hours. Profit: ₹40 on A and ₹50 on B.

Let x units of A and y units of B be made. Maximise Z = 40x + 50y subject to 2x + y ≤ 40, x + 3y ≤ 45, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

notes.heading: Graphical (corner point) method
notes.html:
1. Treat each constraint as an equation and draw its line using intercepts.
  2. Shade the correct side of each line (test with the origin when the line does not pass through it).
  3. Mark the feasible region and find its corner points (solve pairs of equations for intersections).
  4. Evaluate Z at every corner point.
  5. For a bounded region, the largest value is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum.

Fundamental theorem: if an optimal value exists, it occurs at a corner point of the feasible region.

notes.heading: Worked example: maximisation
notes.html:
Solve Example 1. Lines: 2x + y = 40 through (20, 0) and (0, 40); x + 3y = 45 through (45, 0) and (0, 15). Intersection: y = 40 − 2x → x + 120 − 6x = 45 → x = 15, y = 10.

Corner pointZ = 40x + 50y
O (0, 0)0
A (20, 0)800
B (15, 10)1,100
C (0, 15)750

Maximum profit is ₹1,100 when 15 units of A and 10 units of B are made.

notes.heading: Worked example: minimisation
notes.html:
Minimise Z = 200x + 500y subject to x + 2y ≥ 10, 3x + 4y ≤ 24, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

Lines: x + 2y = 10 through (10, 0), (0, 5); 3x + 4y = 24 through (8, 0), (0, 6). Intersection: x = 10 − 2y → 30 − 6y + 4y = 24 → y = 3, x = 4.

The feasible region lies above the first line and below the second, with x ≥ 0: a triangle.

Corner pointZ = 200x + 500y
(0, 5)2,500
(4, 3)2,300
(0, 6)3,000

Minimum Z = 2,300 at (4, 3).

notes.heading: Special cases
notes.html:
• Unbounded feasible region: a maximum may not exist. For a minimum m found at a corner, check the open half-plane ax + by < m: if it has no point in common with the feasible region, m is the minimum; otherwise there is no minimum. (Similarly use ax + by > M for a maximum.)
  • Multiple optimal solutions: if two adjacent corner points give the same optimal Z, every point on the segment joining them is optimal.
  • Infeasible problem: the constraints have no common region, so there is no solution.

notes.heading: Common mistakes
notes.html:
• Shading the wrong side of a line: always test a point.
  • Missing a corner point where a constraint line meets an axis.
  • Reading intersection points off the graph instead of solving the equations.
  • Forgetting non-negativity restrictions.
  • Declaring a maximum for an unbounded region without the half-plane check.

The set of all points satisfying every constraint, including non-negativity.
Any point inside or on the boundary of the feasible region.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): An LPP with an unbounded feasible region may still have a minimum value.
Reason (R): Every LPP has an optimal solution.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: A is true (check with the open half-plane). R is false: infeasible or unbounded problems may have no optimal solution.

questions.q: Define the feasible region of an LPP.
questions.answerHtml: It is the common region determined by all the constraints, including the non-negativity restrictions, of the problem.

questions.q: A tailor earns ₹150 on a shirt and ₹200 on a trouser. He can stitch at most 12 garments a day and must stitch at least 2 trousers. Formulate the LPP to maximise his earnings.
questions.answerHtml:
Let x shirts and y trousers be stitched daily.

Maximise Z = 150x + 200y subject to x + y ≤ 12, y ≥ 2, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

questions.q: Maximise Z = 5x + 3y subject to 3x + 5y ≤ 15, 5x + 2y ≤ 10, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
Minimise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 8, 3x + 5y ≤ 15, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
questions.answerHtml:
3x + 5y ≤ 15 with x, y ≥ 0 is the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (5, 0), (0, 3). For every point in it, x + y ≤ 5.

But x + y ≥ 8 is required. The two regions have no common point, so the feasible region is empty.

The problem is infeasible: there is no solution.

questions.q: Case study: A dietician mixes foods P and Q. Each kg of P has 2 units of vitamin A and 1 unit of vitamin C; each kg of Q has 1 unit of A and 2 units of C. The mixture must have at least 8 units of A and 10 units of C. P costs ₹50 per kg and Q costs ₹70 per kg. Find the least-cost mixture.
questions.answerHtml:
Let x kg of P and y kg of Q be used. Minimise Z = 50x + 70y subject to 2x + y ≥ 8, x + 2y ≥ 10, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

Lines: 2x + y = 8 through (4, 0), (0, 8); x + 2y = 10 through (10, 0), (0, 5). Intersection: y = 8 − 2x → x + 16 − 4x = 10 → x = 2, y = 4.

The feasible region is unbounded with corner points (0, 8), (2, 4), (10, 0).

CornerZ = 50x + 70y
(0, 8)560
(2, 4)380
(10, 0)500

Since the region is unbounded, check 50x + 70y < 380: this half-plane has no point in common with the feasible region. Hence the minimum cost is ₹380, using 2 kg of P and 4 kg of Q.
